notes: DLP (Barrow) in ruling slot 3 (MD had DLP in 2, BLP in 3); BLP moved to slot 2 as the moderate opposition, conservative Barbados National Party in slot 1. No real coalition partner existed; slot 18 holds the Barbados Workers' Union. Barbados Defence Force dates from 1979, so slot 22 is the Barbados Regiment.

0.name: Special Branch
0.text:
The Special Branch is the political intelligence section of the Royal Barbados Police Force, created in colonial times and retained after independence in 1966. In 1970 its officers monitor Black Power speakers, visiting radicals from Trinidad and the United States, and the study groups at the Cave Hill campus of the University of the West Indies.

Its culture is that of the Cold War and of British policing: suspicion of communism, close liaison with London and Washington, and a preference for banning orders and deportations over debate. Its leverage lies in surveillance files, immigration control and the ear of the cabinet.

1.name: Barbados National Party
1.text:
The Barbados National Party is the heir of the old conservative Electors' Association, the party of the planters and merchants of Bridgetown who dominated the colonial House of Assembly. Led by the former Bridgetown mayor Ernest Mottley, it won only two seats at independence in 1966 and is a declining force in 1970.

It stands for private enterprise, low taxes, the plantation economy, firm order and the closest ties with Britain, the Crown and the United States. It opposes Black Power and distrusts Barrow's activist state. Its leverage lies in white and near-white business families, church networks and the economic weight of its backers.

2.name: Barbados Labour Party
2.text:
The Barbados Labour Party, founded in 1938 as the Barbados Progressive League, is the oldest mass party on the island. Its founder, Sir Grantley Adams, led Barbados through universal suffrage and served as Prime Minister of the short-lived West Indies Federation; since 1966 he has led the opposition, with younger men such as his son Tom Adams pressing for renewal.

The BLP has moved from Fabian labourism toward a moderate, business-friendly reformism, stressing good governance, fiscal caution, civil liberties and close ties with Britain and the United States. Its leverage lies in its history, the professional classes and a loyal base in the parishes.

3.name: Democratic Labour Party
3.text:
The Democratic Labour Party was founded in 1955 by dissidents from the Barbados Labour Party, among them Errol Barrow, a former RAF navigator and lawyer. Barrow became Premier in 1961 and led Barbados to independence on 30 November 1966; on 1 January 1970 he is Prime Minister and Minister of Finance at the head of a confident government.

The DLP stands for free secondary education, social security, industrial development, tourism and a mixed economy under an active state. It is Western in alignment but insists on sovereignty, Caribbean integration through CARIFTA and friendship with all. Its leverage lies in Barrow's authority, the civil service and the rural and working-class vote.

4.name: Cave Hill Study Circle
4.text:
The Cave Hill Study Circle is the name for the handful of lecturers, students and young professionals who read Marx, Lenin and Fanon at the Cave Hill campus of the University of the West Indies, opened in 1963. In 1970 they have no party, publish cyclostyled sheets and debate in rum shops and seminar rooms.

They argue that independence has left power with the planters and foreign capital and that only a disciplined workers' party, linked to Cuba and the socialist camp, can complete decolonisation. They want nationalised sugar, land reform and a planned economy. Their leverage lies in the classroom, the press and trade-union education classes.

5.name: Black Star Circle
5.text:
The Black Star Circle gathers the young Barbadians who answer the Black Power call ringing across the Caribbean after the Rodney riots in Jamaica in 1968 and the Montreal student protests of 1969. Students, unemployed youths and returned migrants wear dashikis, read Garvey and Stokely Carmichael and hold street meetings in Bridgetown.

They denounce white control of land, commerce and tourism, call for African consciousness and economic power for Black Barbadians, and reject both the DLP and the BLP as Afro-Saxon elites. Their leverage lies in youth, music and the threat of unrest, which the government watches nervously.

6.name: Bim First
6.text:
Bim First is the slogan of an old-guard nationalist milieu of shopkeepers, preachers, small planters and labour veterans who feel that independence has merely swapped British masters for American tourists, Canadian banks and foreign hotel chains. They meet in parish halls and rum shops and write angry letters to the Advocate.

They want Barbadian ownership of land and business, curbs on foreign investment and on the sale of beachfront to outsiders, and a foreign policy that keeps Washington and London at arm's length. Socially they are deeply conservative, hostile to permissiveness and Black Power alike. Their leverage lies in parish pride and the rural churches.

7.name: Dipper's Men
7.text:
Dipper's Men, named after Errol Barrow's nickname, are the ministers, party organisers and senior officials who see the Prime Minister as the indispensable architect of the new nation. In 1970 they control the DLP machine, the government boards and the patronage that flows from new schools, roads and hotels.

They favour a strong executive, a disciplined dominant party and an independent, Third World foreign policy that would open relations with Cuba and other non-Western states. Impatient with parliamentary obstruction and a hostile press, they would tighten public order law. Their leverage lies in Barrow's popularity and their hold on the state.

8.name: Ahl al-Bayt Circle
8.text:
The Ahl al-Bayt Circle is a small group of Shia Muslims in Bridgetown, mostly Indian migrants from Trinidad and Guyana who brought the Hosay devotion with them, joined by a few students following the Lebanese cleric Musa al-Sadr. In 1970 they meet privately during Muharram and keep a low profile beside the Sunni Gujarati community.

They want recognition as a distinct religious community, freedom to commemorate Ashura publicly and closer ties to the wider Shia world. Their politics are reformist and peaceful, combining religious revival with social justice. Their leverage is negligible beyond a few families and their links to Trinidad.

9.name: Hussaini Brothers
9.text:
The Hussaini Brothers are a tight-knit handful of devout young Shia men in Bridgetown, sons of Indian migrant families, who reject the folk festivities of Hosay and look to the clergy of Najaf and Qom for guidance. In 1970 they correspond with seminaries abroad and gather for strict mourning rites in a private house.

They hold that society should be ordered by religious law and led by learned clerics, and regard Western culture and the tourist economy as corrupting. Their numbers are tiny and their politics untested, but their discipline and foreign links give them a voice among the island's few Shia families.

10.name: Bridgetown Mosque
10.text:
The Bridgetown Mosque on Kensington New Road, completed in the 1950s, is the centre of Barbados's small Muslim community, made up largely of Gujarati traders from Surat and Bharuch who arrived from the 1910s onward. In 1970 its trustees are respected merchants of Swan Street and the dry-goods trade.

The mosque's elders stand for orthodox Sunni practice, religious instruction for their children, discreet good relations with the government and ties to Muslim scholars in India and the Arabian peninsula. They avoid politics and value stability above all. Their leverage lies in commercial wealth and in the cohesion of the community.

11.name: Brothers of the Ummah
11.text:
The Brothers of the Ummah are a tiny circle of Afro-Barbadian converts and returned migrants from New York and London who encountered Islam through Malcolm X and the Black Power movement. In 1970 they pray together in rented rooms in Bridgetown, sell pamphlets and preach to young men in the poorer districts.

They teach that the Muslim world must unite under one Islamic authority and that the Caribbean's colonial order can only be overthrown by Islam. They reject parliamentary politics and both superpowers. Their influence is minimal, but their message of dignity and discipline appeals to unemployed youth and prisoners.

12.name: Young Muslims of Swan Street
12.text:
The Young Muslims of Swan Street are the educated sons of the Gujarati merchant families, many schooled in Britain or India, who gather for study circles above the family shops in Bridgetown. In 1970 they read Mawdudi and Hasan al-Banna and want a more active, organised faith than their fathers practise.

They call for Islamic schooling, charity, moral reform and engagement with Barbadian society, presenting Islam as a modern and complete way of life. They respect the law and the constitution and hope to build a recognised Muslim association. Their leverage lies in education, family wealth and links to Islamic movements abroad.

13.name: Barbados Civil Service
13.text:
The Barbados Civil Service, trained in the British tradition and proud of its reputation as the most efficient in the Commonwealth Caribbean, runs the new state's ministries, statutory boards and development plans. In 1970 its permanent secretaries and planners manage the expansion of schools, tourism and the industrial estates under Barrow's ministers.

Its senior officers favour orderly, rational administration, continuity across governments and pragmatic relations with East and West. They are wary of party patronage and street politics alike. Their leverage lies in expertise, procedure and the dependence of every minister on their files.

14.name: Anglican Diocese of Barbados
14.text:
The Anglican Diocese of Barbados is the island's largest church and was the established state church until its disestablishment in 1969. Its parish churches, bishop and rectors remain woven into the fabric of rural and middle-class life, and the Bishop of Barbados is still a public figure of the first rank in 1970.

The church stands for Christian moral order, family, education in church schools and respect for the Crown and constitution. It is cautious about Black Power, communism and permissive culture, but increasingly concerned with poverty and race. Its leverage lies in its eleven parishes, its schools and the loyalty of older Barbadians.

15.name: Barbados Sugar Producers' Association
15.text:
The Barbados Sugar Producers' Association speaks for the plantation owners who still hold much of the island's best land, a white elite descended from the old plantocracy and allied with the 'Big Six' merchant houses of Bridgetown. In 1970 sugar remains the leading export, though tourism is catching up fast.

The planters want guaranteed markets under the Commonwealth Sugar Agreement, cheap labour, low taxes and no land reform. They are staunchly pro-British and anti-socialist, and dislike Barrow's taxes and labour laws. Their leverage lies in land, credit, family networks and their seats on banking and commercial boards.

16.name: Barbados Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Barbados Chamber of Commerce, founded in 1825, is one of the oldest business associations in the Americas and represents the merchants, importers, hoteliers and new manufacturers of the island. In 1970 its members are expanding into tourism, real estate and light industry under Barrow's incentive laws.

The Chamber preaches free enterprise, low duties, light regulation, sound money and open doors to North American investment and tourists. It distrusts union militancy and state ownership. Its leverage lies in the commercial wealth of Bridgetown, its links to foreign banks and its weight as an employer.

17.name: Barbados National Trust
17.text:
The Barbados National Trust was founded in 1961 to preserve the island's historic buildings, plantation houses, gardens and natural sites. Its members, drawn from old families, teachers, architects and naturalists, are campaigning in 1970 to save Georgian Bridgetown, the gullies and the coastline from unchecked hotel and road building.

The Trust wants protected landscapes, planning controls, conservation of the reefs and the Scotland District, and respect for the island's heritage amid the tourist boom. It is genteel and non-partisan in style. Its leverage lies in expertise, social standing and access to ministers and the press.

18.name: Barbados Workers' Union
18.text:
The Barbados Workers' Union, founded in 1941 out of the labour movement of Grantley Adams, is the largest union on the island, organising sugar, port, hotel and public workers. It has been led since 1948 by General Secretary Frank Walcott, a powerful orator and a figure in national politics in his own right.

The BWU stands for collective bargaining, social security, decent wages in sugar and tourism, and a labour voice in national development, without tying itself to either bloc. It shifts between the two main parties as its members' interests demand. Its leverage lies in the canefields, the harbour and the hotels.

19.name: Clement Payne Circle
19.text:
The Clement Payne Circle honours the Trinidad-born organiser whose deportation from Barbados in 1937 sparked the riots that gave birth to the island's labour movement. Its members in 1970 are radical teachers, dockworkers and young intellectuals who believe the labour parties have betrayed Payne's legacy.

They favour an independent Caribbean Marxism that owes nothing to Moscow or Beijing: workers' control, land for the landless, the end of the plantation and a federation of socialist Caribbean states. They reject the Westminster parties as instruments of the merchant elite. Their leverage lies in historical memory and the rank and file of the unions.

20.name: Little England League
20.text:
The Little England League takes its name from the island's old boast of being the most English of the colonies, and rallies conservative small businessmen, civil-service pensioners, rural churchgoers and some white and near-white families. In 1970 it is a loose network of letter-writers, club members and parish notables.

It calls for law and order, a crackdown on Black Power agitators, curbs on migrants from the smaller islands and protection of traditional values and institutions against what it sees as reckless change. It is loudly loyal to the Crown and the West. Its leverage lies in anxieties about crime and unemployment.

21.name: Plantation Guard
21.text:
The Plantation Guard is the name whispered for a fringe of hardline planters, ex-officers of the colonial volunteer forces and a few businessmen who never accepted the end of planter rule. In 1970 they meet at private estates and clubs, keep firearms and correspond with sympathisers in Rhodesia and South Africa.

They want an end to party politics, emergency powers, the suppression of unions and Black Power, and a government of 'responsible' men backed by force. They scorn both independence and democracy. Their numbers are tiny and their ideas despised, but their wealth and connections to the police give them a dangerous reach.

22.name: Barbados Regiment
22.text:
The Barbados Regiment is the island's small military force, descended from colonial volunteer units and re-formed in 1948, now serving the independent state as a largely part-time body around a regular cadre. In 1970 it numbers only a few hundred men, and the police remain the main instrument of internal security.

Its British-trained officers regard themselves as apolitical servants of the Crown and constitution and look to Britain, Canada and the United States for training and equipment. The regiment's leverage is modest, but in a small island state any organised armed force carries weight in a crisis.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
The House of Windsor reigns over Barbados through Queen Elizabeth II, who became Queen of Barbados at independence on 30 November 1966. Her representative, Governor-General Sir Winston Scott, the first Barbadian to hold the office, exercises her powers on the advice of Errol Barrow's cabinet.

The Crown embodies three centuries of parliamentary continuity, the Westminster system and the Commonwealth link, and the Privy Council remains the final court of appeal. Loyalty is deep among older Barbadians, the Anglican establishment and the business elite. Its leverage lies in constitutional legitimacy and the Governor-General's reserve powers.
